display_title: Maybe better as a workshop paper?

content.comment:
The entire paper is based off of one equation, typically representative of workshop submissions.

Compared to other papers presented in this conference (including those in the area of catastrophic forgetting), the authors do not go beyond MNIST problem sets to validate their work. Large infrastructure was not needed for evaluation, hence it is even more disappointing. 

The analysis presented under Section 3 does not offer any "unique" insights into the catastrophic forgetting problem. The second "freezing" method seems to be trivial and not explored in much depth at all.

There are some notation issues (ref equation tree at the end of page 3).

Wishing the authors the best of luck !

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper introduces a framework for combatting catastrophic forgetting, based upon changing the loss term to minimise changes in classifier likelihood, obtained via a Taylor series approximation. They compare different versions of their method with EWC and a method based on freezing important weights on three benchmarks.

I like the core concept that the paper proposes. It is explained well, and the paper is well-written. It is interesting to see EWC explained in this framework. However, although the paper starts off with some nice theory (Equations 1 and 2), it then becomes a heavily empirical paper, with many seemingly arbitrary decisions made (and only some high-level comments provided explaining them), for example for Case II and IV, and for the 'constrained' method. Why were these changes to the loss function made? Can they be justified somehow theoretically?

I also have some misgivings regarding the experiments, as they are only performed on MNIST-sized datasets. The proposed method should (if I understand correctly) be scalable to larger datasets/architectures, which most other works in this field do. Additionally, other methods (there are many, but for example VCL [1]) significantly out-perform the proposed method.

I am on the fence about this paper. Although I like the core concept and some of the experimental ideas (such as the 'freezing' method), this paper makes many decisions about its loss function that I do not understand theoretically. Doing this means that empirical results should be strong to back up these decisions, but the experiments are only on MNIST and, although they out-perform EWC, do not out-perform other continual learning works. This means that I am leaning towards reject. I hope to see a future version on this paper with improvements!

[1] Nguyen et al. Variational continual learning. ICML, 2018.

content.review: In this paper, the authors try to solve continual learning prolem, which is a longstanding goal of AI. There are 3 ways to mitigate forgetting: 1. architectrual approaches, 2. regularization approaches, 3. memory approaches. The authors focus on the second one, that is, reguarization approaches. In order to mitigate catastrophic forgetting problem, L_2 strategies was proposed previously. In this paper, they use L_1 strategy instead. I think the mothod is not novel, which does not reach the level of ICLR.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
The paper studies the problem of catastrophic forgetting and proposes a number of methods for overcoming this issue, under various circumstances. The crux of the proposed methods is the a criterion in eq. 1 for minimizing the change in likelihood over the previous datasets. The authors use this as a regularization term and compare and contrast various versions of it with previous work such as EWC.

On the surface of it, the proposed method(s) are sensible, though if I understand things correctly, the main proposed criterion (eq 2) is very similar in shape to EWC, with the main change being L1 vs L2. I can buy that L1 produces different solutions compared to L2, as argued by the authors around eq. 2, so that's fine. On the other hand, I find the contribution of this work relatively minimal. The dissection of case I-IV is good though these are basically small iterations of eq. 1. If I understand it correctly, most (all?) of the cases could have been analyzed with an L2 penalty instead of L1 -- I think this would have added some value to the overall theme of L1 being a better choice  than L2, no?

A few other comments:

* I have a small but potentially important reservation about the experimental protocol -- I don't see any mention of a validation set, it's not clear to me how the hyper-parameters were actually chosen?
* While I appreciate the stds being provided over 5 seeds, there are many cases in which the confidence ranges between various methods actually overlap: this is not made clear in the tables themselves (there are cases in which the proposed methods overlap in confidence intervals with the other baselines)
* There's some discussion in section 6 about the magnitudes of optimal L1 and L2 hparams found by the authors, but I don't know if the "stronger" lambda is really an indication of anything (it could be due to optimization quirks related to gradient descent).
* Are the baseline results (EWC and SI) lifted from the previous papers or done by the authors themselves? It's not immediately clear.
* I don't know how excited I should be about the fact that all results are on variations of MNIST, it does not instill a lot of confidence that these results would generalize to other domains.
* I would have liked the authors to create at least some toy examples or datasets where the proposed methods should shine -- right now it just looks like a list of four semi-sensible alternatives that are basically treated as hyper-parameters in the results table and it's not obvious why someone would choose one of these vs another.

All in all, I can see some value to this work -- certainly a relatively small modification that has some practical benefits, but I'd like to see this better positioned -- empirically, especially -- and better analyzed (cf. my comments about L2).

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable comments and suggestions. We respond to the major points below.

… the main proposed criterion (eq 2) is very similar in shape to EWC … (Review #4)
We agree that the proposed criterion is similar in shape to EWC, however the per-parameter importances are not the Fisher importances, but a different expectation. The overall loss (whether using the L1 or L2 variant) is weaker than the loss obtained through the KL-approximation, which EWC uses. This increases the model variance and allows for a greater span of solutions.

… most (all?) of the cases could have been analyzed with an L2 penalty instead of L1 … (Review #4)
We agree. We have since conducted experiments with the L2 variant and will include them in a future submission.

… I don't see any mention of a validation set, it's not clear to me how the hyper-parameters were actually chosen? … (Review #4)
All the average accuracies refer to average validation accuracies. We chose the hyperparameter by running the experiment for a single seed and choosing the hyperparameter corresponding to the highest average validation accuracy, then repeat the experiments for 5 seeds. We have made this more explicit in the manuscript.

… there are many cases in which the confidence ranges between various methods actually overlap … (Review #4)
Some of the evaluated methods are sensitive to seeds. We consider a method as better if it performs better on average across several seeds, and acknowledge that we should have mentioned this. Note that in most cases, even though the confidence ranges overlap, the method with the lower mean also has a higher variance. In this case, having a higher mean and lower variance of solution clearly indicates superiority.

… I don't know if the "stronger" lambda is really an indication of anything (it could be due to optimization quirks related to gradient descent) … (Review #4)
The stronger lambda does correspond to a stronger constraint (a stronger spring, for example in EWC) on the solution that can be found by the optimizer. We will clarify this in a future submission.

… Are the baseline results (EWC and SI) lifted from the previous papers or done by the authors themselves? … (Review #4)
None of the results were taken from previous papers, since they don’t necessarily use the same datasets or same number of tasks. For SI, the original authors released the code, so we just ran that on our datasets. We will make this clear in the manuscript.

… all results are on variations of MNIST, it does not instill a lot of confidence that these results would generalize to other domains … (Review #4)
We have since done some CIFAR100 experiments and we are indeed able to get the same trends.

… create at least some toy examples or datasets … (Review #4)
Why were these changes to the loss function made? (Review # 5)
We agree that the changes to the loss function could have been justified better, perhaps through figures or toy examples.

Additionally, other methods (there are many, but for example VCL [1]) significantly out-perform the proposed method. (Review #5)
Our goal was to compare the effect of our approach with regularized continual learning methods that use a fixed capacity, hence the choice of EWC and SI, which are the two most popular methods in that area following that assumption. VCL may out-perform the proposed method, but it uses a multi-head discriminative network (refer to Figure 1 in the VCL paper), which means the capacity is not fixed.

… In order to mitigate catastrophic forgetting problem, L_2 strategies was proposed previously. In this paper, they use L_1 strategy instead. … (Review #2)
A lot of the previous methods have been L_2 strategies, but with different effects. An L_2 strategy is any constraint that looks like $\sum_{j} k_j (\theta_j - \theta_j^*)^2$. EWC, SI, EWC++ and other methods in the literature satisfy this form, which is a weighted L_2 loss. Our method uses a different $k_j$ than these methods and has a different form, which has not been done before. Also note that these weighted strategies are different from the L_2 mentioned in EWC (which they use as a baseline), which is an unweighted L_2 loss. We will make this more explicit in a future submission.

Although we will update the manuscript in line with the above responses, we feel that our work will benefit significantly by the inclusion of more examples and experiments, as suggested by the reviewers. Unfortunately, this will constitute too big of a change for the current submission and we must regretfully withdraw our manuscript.
